stemBlocks.value: A group of 120 students recorded how they travelled to school; the pie chart shows Walk 90°, Bus 144°, Bicycle 54° and Car x°. (a) Calculate the value of x. (b) Calculate the percentage of students who travelled by bus. (c) Determine the number of students who travelled by car. (d) Find the probability that a student chosen at random travelled by neither walking nor bus. (e) State the modal method of travel.
Think first: Every part rests on one fact: the four sector angles must add to 360°.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p079-q06 from workbook page 79.

solutionSteps.instruction: Subtract the three known angles from 360°.
Turn the bus angle into a percentage.
Turn the car angle into a number of students.
Add the angles of the categories that are neither walking nor bus.
Write that angle as a probability.

strategyBlocks.value: Find x from the 360° total, then convert each angle to a fraction of 360 to obtain percentages, numbers of students and probabilities.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (a) x = 72  (b) 40%  (c) 24 students  (d) 7/20 or 0.35  (e) Bus, which has the largest sector at 144°.

whyThisWorks.value: A pie chart shares 360° in the same ratio as the data, so an angle out of 360 is the same fraction as a category out of the total. That single equivalence lets you move freely between angles, percentages, numbers of students and probabilities.

commonErrors.misconception: Subtracting from 180° instead of 360° when finding x.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Subtracting from 180° instead of 360° when finding x.

commonErrors.misconception: Dividing the angle by 120 instead of by 360 when finding the number of students.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Dividing the angle by 120 instead of by 360 when finding the number of students.

commonErrors.misconception: Reading 'neither walking nor bus' as one remaining category instead of both.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Reading 'neither walking nor bus' as one remaining category instead of both.

examTip.value: On any pie chart, first work out what one degree is worth (here 120 ÷ 360 of a student per degree) — then every sector converts in a single multiplication.
